unit.title: Crypto risks and reality
unit.description: Volatility, collapses, scams, yields and how much crypto weighs in a portfolio

steps.title: Falls of 70 % or more
steps.body:
Bitcoin has suffered several falls of more than 70 % from its highs:

• **2014-2015:** more than 80 %.
• **2018:** more than 80 %.
• **2022:** more than 75 %.

Winning back its late-2017 high took about **3 years**; its November 2021 high, more than **2 years** (March 2024). Many other cryptos fell more than 90 % and never came back.

steps.title: How much it has to rise to recover
steps.body: Set the loss at 75 %: it takes a 300 % rise to get back to where you started. Try it with 90 %.
steps.tip: That's why big falls hurt so much: recovering means multiplying.

steps.title: Volatility in numbers
steps.body: Bitcoin's annual volatility is around **50-80 %**, compared with 15 % for a global stock index. A −10 % week is common. It's a highly volatile asset, no guarantee scheme covers it and **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: In crypto, falls of 70 % and years of waiting to recover are part of the history.
steps.tip: If something can rise 300 % in a year, it can also fall 75 %.

steps.title: What happened
steps.body:
**FTX** was one of the biggest exchanges in the world. In **November 2022** it emerged that **Alameda Research**, a sister company owned by its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, relied heavily on FTX's token (FTT) and that FTX had passed customers' money to it.

Customers rushed to withdraw, FTX **froze withdrawals** on 8 November and filed for **bankruptcy** on the 11th.

steps.title: Counterparty risk
steps.body:
When you leave your crypto on a platform you take on **counterparty risk**: you depend on that company being solvent and honest. If it mixes your money with its own and goes bust, you become just another creditor in a process that lasts years.

In 2024 Bankman-Fried was sentenced to **25 years** in prison for fraud.

steps.title: What changed
steps.body: MiCA now requires platforms to be authorised and to keep customers' assets separate. Even so, in crypto there's no guarantee scheme like the one for bank deposits: it pays to know who holds your crypto and not to keep it all on one platform. And remember: **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: If someone else holds your crypto, you also take on their risk of bankruptcy or fraud.
steps.tip: Even a huge exchange can collapse in a week.

steps.title: Memecoins
steps.body:
A **memecoin** is a cryptocurrency born from a joke or a trend (Dogecoin started in 2013 as a joke). Many have no use at all: their price depends only on attention.

Creating a token takes minutes and very little money. Thousands appear every day, and the vast majority end up worth almost nothing.

steps.title: How they rob you
steps.body:
• **Rug pull:** the creators attract money and vanish, selling everything or pulling the liquidity. The SQUID token (2021) shot up and within minutes fell to almost zero; on top of that, buyers couldn't sell.
• ***Pump and dump*:** a group inflates the price with hype and sells to latecomers.
• **Fake airdrops:** "claim your free tokens" by connecting your wallet… and you sign a permission that lets them empty it.

steps.title: The red flags
steps.body: Anonymous creators with no track record, promises of "x100", urgency, paid influencers, not being able to sell, being asked to connect your wallet or share your seed phrase. With these tokens **you can lose everything you invest** in minutes.
steps.key: If the only reason to buy is that "it's going to go up", someone probably wants to sell to you.
steps.tip: With a memecoin, your money may be someone else's exit.

u13l4.title: Staking and DeFi: where the yield comes from

steps.title: Staking
steps.body:
On **proof-of-stake** networks (like Ethereum), people who lock up their coins to validate blocks get a reward: that's **staking**.

This yield comes from **new coins** and network **fees**, and it's paid in the same crypto: if it falls 50 %, a small annual yield won't make up for it. If the validator misbehaves, it can lose part of the stake (*slashing*).

steps.title: DeFi and crypto lending
steps.body:
In **DeFi** you lend your crypto to others through smart contracts: the borrower pays you. Some centralised platforms that promised high interest, like Celsius, went bust in 2022.

Risks: bugs in the code, hacks, platforms that use your money, and the price falling.

steps.title: The question that sums it all up
steps.body: **Who pays the interest, and why?** If nobody can explain it, the interest may be coming out of newcomers' money. In 2022 one platform paid almost 20 % for depositing the UST stablecoin thanks to subsidies: when they were no longer enough, the whole thing collapsed. In crypto **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Every yield comes from somewhere: if you don't know where, maybe the yield is you.
steps.tip: High, "risk-free" interest doesn't exist: either there's risk or there's a scam.

steps.title: Two ways to hold crypto
steps.body:
• **Directly:** you buy the crypto on an exchange and either you or the platform holds it. It trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
• **Through the stock market:** you buy a listed product that tracks its price, with your usual broker and during market hours.

In the US, **spot bitcoin ETFs** were approved in January 2024.

steps.title: In Europe: ETPs and ETNs
steps.body:
UCITS rules don't allow a fund holding a single crypto, so in Europe they're sold as **ETPs** or **ETNs**: debt securities from an issuer, usually **backed** by the crypto held by a custodian.

Risks: those of the crypto (all of them) plus those of the issuer and the custodian. And they charge an annual fee. Many US ETFs can't be bought from the EU because they don't have a KID.

steps.title: The same price risk
steps.body: The wrapper changes the custody, the trading hours and the paperwork, **not the volatility**: if bitcoin falls 70 %, so does the ETP. According to Morningstar, investors in bitcoin ETFs earned about 14 points a year less than the ETFs themselves by buying on the way up and selling on the way down. **You can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: A crypto ETP saves you from looking after keys, but it doesn't save you a single point of volatility.
steps.tip: The wrapper doesn't change what's inside.

u13l6.title: How much crypto in a portfolio

steps.title: Think about the whole
steps.body:
The question isn't "how much could this crypto go up?" but **what happens to my whole portfolio if it falls 75 %?**

With 5 % in crypto, a 75 % fall takes **3.75 %** off the total. With 50 %, it takes off **37.5 %**. The weight decides how much it hurts.

steps.title: How to reason about it
steps.body:
People who decide to hold crypto usually write into their plan:

• First, the **safety cushion** and no expensive debt.
• A **maximum**: a small percentage they could lose entirely without it changing their life.
• When to **rebalance**: if it goes over the maximum, sell the excess.

These are examples of how to think about it, not personalised recommendations.

steps.title: The part you could lose
steps.body: If crypto takes off, its weight grows by itself and your portfolio becomes riskier without you deciding anything. In crypto **you can lose everything you invest**: the percentage you choose should be one you could bear to see go to zero.
steps.key: Crypto's weight in the total, not its potential, decides how much it can hurt you.
steps.tip: Write down your crypto maximum today, before a rally talks you out of it.

u13l1-1.prompt: November 2021: Bitcoin has risen almost 7-fold since May 2020 and is hitting all-time highs. Many say "this time it's different". What did it do over the following year?
u13l1-1.explanation: After such strong rises, the risk of a big fall is also high. This episode is one of the most studied examples of crypto volatility.

u13l1-2.prompt: One of the big cryptocurrencies, in daily candlesticks. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u13l1-2.explanation: In crypto, moves of 10-15 % in two weeks are common, in either direction.

u13l1-3.prompt: Another big cryptocurrency, in daily candlesticks. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u13l1-3.explanation: Guessing the next move of such a volatile asset is a lot like tossing a coin.

u13l1-4.prompt: Bitcoin falls 75 % from its high. How much does it then need to rise to get back there?
u13l1-4.explanation: If 100 becomes 25, getting back to 100 means multiplying by 4: a 300 % rise.

u13l1-5.prompt: You invest €2,000 in a cryptocurrency and it falls 84 %, like Bitcoin in 2018. How much do you have left?

u13l1-6.prompt: A cryptocurrency falls 90 %. How much does it need to rise to get back to its high?
u13l1-6.explanation: From 100 to 10: getting back to 100 means multiplying by 10, a 900 % rise.

u13l1-7.explanation: Compared with 15 % for a global stock index.

u13l1-8.prompt: Laura bought bitcoin at a peak and is down 60 %. She reads on social media that "it always recovers". What does she think?
options: That she doesn't know if or when it will recover, so she decides based on her plan and what she can afford to lose
That she should take out a loan to buy more and average down
That it will definitely recover, as always
u13l1-8.explanation: When prices drop sharply, what helps is a plan made calmly, not slogans from social media.
feedback: Good: in crypto you can lose everything you invest; that's why position size is decided beforehand.
Borrowing for an asset that may keep falling can turn a loss into a serious problem.
Bitcoin has recovered in the past after years; many other cryptos never have. The past guarantees nothing.

u13l1-9.prompt: After the 2022 crash, Bitcoin took more than 2 years to get back to its November 2021 high.
u13l1-9.explanation: It passed it in March 2024. Many other cryptos from that time have never returned to their highs.

u13l1-10.prompt: Order from lowest to highest typical volatility.
u13l1-10.explanation: Less than 1 %, 4-7 %, around 15 % and 50-80 % a year.

u13l2-1.prompt: Put in order what happened with FTX in November 2022.
options: It's reported that Alameda, its sister company, relies heavily on the FTT token
u13l2-1.explanation: It all happened in about ten days: trust took years to build and days to break.

options: The risk of the price falling
The risk that whoever holds or owes you your money can't or won't give it back
The risk of sending to the wrong address
u13l2-2.explanation: It doesn't depend on the asset, but on the company you're trusting.

u13l2-3.prompt: If you leave your crypto on an exchange that goes bust, a guarantee scheme pays you back up to €100,000.
u13l2-3.explanation: That scheme exists for bank deposits; there's nothing equivalent for crypto.

u13l2-4.prompt: FTX used its customers' money at Alameda Research, a company linked to its founder.
u13l2-4.explanation: Mixing customers' money with the company's own was the key to the fraud.

u13l2-5.prompt: Bruno keeps all his crypto on an exchange that pays 8 % for leaving it there. He reads rumours of trouble and sees withdrawals are taking days. What would someone who has learnt from FTX do?
options: Check whether it's authorised and how it holds the assets, and not keep everything in one place
Deposit more to make the most of the 8 %
Wait: it's a big exchange, it can't fail
u13l2-5.explanation: Slow withdrawals and eye-catching yields are warning signs to watch for on any platform.
feedback: Good: knowing your counterparty and not concentrating custody softens the blow if something goes wrong.
If the platform is in trouble, that 8 % is worth nothing.
FTX was huge too, and it collapsed in a week.

u13l2-6.prompt: Ana has €1,000 in crypto on an exchange authorised under MiCA and €9,000 in an index fund. A friend tells her that, after FTX, "all exchanges are scams". What does she reply?
options: That counterparty risk exists, but it's reduced by using authorised platforms, separated assets and not putting everything in one place
That with MiCA the risk is zero
That he's right, and she sells everything
u13l2-6.explanation: Between "it's all a scam" and "there's no risk" lies the useful part: measuring and limiting the risk.
feedback: Good: it doesn't remove the risk, but it limits it. And she knows she could lose that €1,000.
MiCA reduces risks, it doesn't remove them, and it doesn't protect you from price moves.
One platform committing fraud doesn't mean they all do; what's useful is knowing what risk you're taking.

u13l2-7.prompt: Match each case with what it teaches.
u13l2-7.explanation: Three real blows and Europe's regulatory response.
right: An exchange can lose its customers' crypto
Requires authorisation and keeping assets separate
An exchange can misuse its customers' money

u13l2-8.prompt: Quick: what year did FTX go bust?

u13l2-9.prompt: If someone else holds your money, you take on ____ risk.
u13l2-9.explanation: It's the risk that the other party doesn't hold up its end.

u13l2-10.prompt: What reduces counterparty risk in crypto? Select all that apply.
options: Not keeping everything on a single platform
Choosing the one that promises the highest return for deposits
Having your assets kept separate from theirs
u13l2-10.explanation: A high return for deposits usually means the platform is lending out or gambling with your money.

u13l3-1.prompt: Select the messages that are scams or a clear sign of a rug pull.
options: Congratulations, you've got $2,000 in free tokens. Connect your wallet and sign to claim them.
I've read the CNMV guide on crypto-assets, shall we talk about it?

Not financial advice 😉 but I've gone all in on this coin I launched yesterday.
u13l3-1.explanation: Urgency, promises of x100, gifts that ask you to sign and a creator promoting their own coin are classic signs.

u13l3-2.prompt: Which are red flags in a new token? Select all that apply.
options: Its code being published and audited
Not letting you sell after you buy
Anonymous creators with no track record
u13l3-2.explanation: A published audit guarantees nothing, but not having one is a red flag.

u13l3-3.prompt: Match each trap with its definition.
u13l3-3.explanation: Four different traps with the same ending: your money ends up in someone else's pocket.
right: Inflating the price and selling to latecomers
A token that lets you buy but not sell
The creators take the money and vanish

u13l3-4.prompt: Pablo sees a new token that has gone up 2,000 % in two days. In a group chat everyone says there's still plenty of upside. What does he do?
options: Takes out a loan to put in more
Stays out: he doesn't know what it is, who's behind it or whether he'll be able to sell
Puts his savings in: there's still time
u13l3-4.explanation: Buying just because something has gone up a lot is what drives pump and dumps.
feedback: He could end up owing money for something that's no longer worth anything.
Good: if the only argument is that it's going up, the risk of losing everything is huge.
He arrives just as the early buyers want to sell: the classic pump-and-dump victim.

u13l3-5.prompt: Some tokens Laura didn't buy appear in her wallet, and a website offers to swap them for money if she signs an authorisation. What does she do?
options: Doesn't touch those tokens or sign anything
Sells them on any website that will let her
u13l3-5.explanation: In crypto, "free" often costs everything you have in your wallet.
feedback: Good: tokens you didn't ask for are a common bait to get you to sign a malicious permission.
The website that "lets you sell them" is usually the trap.
The signature can give permission to move all her tokens: that's how many fake airdrops work.

options: When a project's creators take the money and abandon it
u13l3-6.explanation: The rug is pulled out from under investors: suddenly there's no floor beneath them.

u13l3-7.prompt: Creating a new token is expensive and difficult, so the ones that exist are usually serious.
u13l3-7.explanation: It takes minutes and very little money: that's why thousands appear every day.

u13l3-8.prompt: If a token won't let you sell after buying it, that's a clear sign of a scam.
u13l3-8.explanation: It's a honeypot: money can only go in.

u13l3-9.explanation: It's the best-known memecoin: its price depends mainly on the attention it gets.

u13l3-10.prompt: Inflating the price with hype to sell to latecomers is called pump and ____.
u13l3-10.explanation: Pump (inflate) and dump (offload): latecomers buy what the organisers are selling.

u13l4-1.prompt: A platform offers a "guaranteed" 25 % a year for depositing your stablecoin. What do you ask first?
options: Can I invite friends to earn more?
What's the most I can deposit?
Who pays that interest, and with what money?
u13l4-1.explanation: Before "how much", ask "where from": that's what separates a real yield from a trap.
feedback: Earning by bringing in others is a typical sign of a pyramid scheme.
First you need to know where the 25 % comes from; if it can't be explained, it may come from newcomers' money.
Good: that's the key question. A bank deposit pays much less because that's the price of money with little risk.

u13l4-2.prompt: Ana stakes a crypto that pays her 3 % a year in that same crypto. Over a year, its price falls 40 %. How has she done?
options: She loses: the staking yield doesn't make up for a 40 % fall
Broke even: staking protects her from falls
Well: she's earned the staking reward
u13l4-2.explanation: A small yield doesn't make up for the volatility of what's underneath.
feedback: Exactly: staking doesn't protect you from the price.
It doesn't protect her: it just adds more units of a coin that has fallen.
The yield is paid in the same crypto: if it falls 40 %, she loses far more than she earns from staking.

u13l4-3.prompt: You stake €1,000 in a crypto that yields 3 % a year in that same crypto. Over a year its price falls 40 %. What's your position worth? (round it)
u13l4-3.explanation: 1,000 × 1.03 × 0.60 = €618. The 3 % doesn't make up for the −40 %.

u13l4-4.prompt: Where does the staking yield come from?
options: From new coins and network fees
u13l4-4.explanation: It's the reward the network pays for validating blocks.

u13l4-5.prompt: In a DeFi loan, the interest you earn is paid by the borrower.
u13l4-5.explanation: That's why the risk also depends on the borrower's collateral and the contract's code.

u13l4-6.prompt: A very high yield in crypto shows the platform is very profitable and safe.
u13l4-6.explanation: It usually means more risk: Celsius went bust in 2022 and UST collapsed after paying almost 20 %.

u13l4-7.prompt: Match each source of yield with who pays it.
u13l4-7.explanation: If you can't fill in this column for a product, you don't know where what you're paid comes from.
right: The bank, which lends that money to others
The network, with new coins and fees

u13l4-8.prompt: What risks come with putting your crypto into DeFi? Select all that apply.
options: The Bank of Spain fining you for using it
u13l4-8.explanation: DeFi risks are technical and market risks; there's no safety net if something goes wrong.

u13l4-9.prompt: The key question for any yield: who ____ the interest?
u13l4-9.explanation: If nobody can explain who pays and why, be wary.

options: You earn more for every friend you bring in
Staking reward on a proof-of-stake network
u13l4-10.explanation: Explainable doesn't mean risk-free, but the unexplainable almost always ends badly.

u13l5-1.prompt: Match each way of getting exposure with its feature.
u13l5-1.explanation: Four routes to the same asset, with different custody risks.
right: The platform holds it for you

u13l5-2.prompt: Buying the crypto directly or an ETP on the stock market?
options: You buy it with your usual broker
Trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week
If you lose your seed phrase, you lose it
u13l5-2.explanation: You swap the risk of self-custody for that of the issuer and the custodian, and add a fee.

u13l5-3.prompt: Why are there no single-cryptocurrency UCITS ETFs in Europe?
options: Because UCITS rules require diversification and don't allow it
Because crypto is banned in Europe
u13l5-3.explanation: That's why single-crypto products are issued as ETPs or ETNs.

u13l5-4.prompt: A bitcoin ETP falls much less than bitcoin because it's listed on a regulated exchange.
u13l5-4.explanation: It tracks bitcoin: if bitcoin falls 70 %, so does the ETP, by roughly the same amount.

u13l5-5.prompt: Pablo wants exposure to bitcoin, but he's afraid of losing his keys. Which option does he consider, and what risk is he left with?
options: An ETP, which removes all risks
A "guaranteed bitcoin fund" someone offers him over the phone
A backed ETP on the stock market: no keys to manage, but he keeps all the volatility and adds the issuer's risk
u13l5-5.explanation: Each way of holding crypto changes which risk you take on, but none removes the price risk.
feedback: It removes the risk of losing your keys, not the risk of bitcoin falling 70 %.
Be wary of any "guarantee" on crypto, especially from someone who calls you out of the blue.
Good: he swaps the risk of self-custody for that of the issuer and the custodian, and the price moves just the same.

u13l5-6.prompt: Bruno buys a bitcoin ETP after it has risen 50 % in a month and sells it in a panic after a 30 % fall. What has happened to him?
options: The behaviour gap: buying in euphoria and selling in panic
He should have bought it directly
He's been unlucky with the product
u13l5-6.explanation: With such volatile assets, the biggest risk is often our own behaviour.
feedback: Exactly: Morningstar estimates that bitcoin ETF investors lost about 14 points a year compared with the ETFs themselves because of this.
The wrapper wouldn't have prevented the fall or his reaction.
The product tracked bitcoin; the problem was when he bought and when he sold.

u13l5-8.explanation: Without a KID, they can't be sold to retail investors in the EU.

u13l5-9.prompt: In Europe, listed products tracking a single crypto are usually ETPs or ____.
u13l5-9.explanation: Exchange Traded Notes: debt securities from the issuer, usually backed by the crypto.

u13l5-10.explanation: The custodian keeps the keys, not you.

u13l6-1.prompt: Split up a sample €10,000 portfolio over 20 years. The written plan says: crypto at most 5 % in total, at least 20 % in bonds and no asset above 60 %.
u13l6-1.explanation: Everyone sets the rules in their own plan; here they're for practice. Note that the crypto limit is bitcoin and ethereum added together.

u13l6-2.prompt: You have €10,000 with 5 % in crypto. Crypto falls 75 % and the rest doesn't move. How much does your portfolio lose in total?

u13l6-3.prompt: Now with 40 % in crypto (4,000 of €10,000). It falls 75 % and the rest doesn't move. What percentage does the portfolio lose?

u13l6-4.prompt: A €10,000 portfolio: €9,500 in funds and €500 in crypto. Crypto triples and the funds don't move. What weight does crypto have now? (one decimal place)
u13l6-4.explanation: 500 × 3 = €1,500; total, €11,000; 1,500 ÷ 11,000 ≈ 13.6 %. It's gone from 5 % to 13.6 % without you deciding anything.

u13l6-5.prompt: Same portfolio: Marta had written down "crypto at most 5 %" and after the rally it's now at 13.6 %. What does she do according to her plan?
options: Puts more money into crypto because it's doing well
Nothing: if it's going up, let it keep going
Rebalances: sells crypto until it's back to 5 % and moves the rest into her funds
u13l6-5.explanation: Rebalancing means following the plan you wrote calmly, not the market's mood.
feedback: That way she's deciding out of euphoria and increasing a risk that was already over her limit.
Her portfolio is now quite a bit riskier than what she calmly decided on.
Good: she sticks to her plan, locks in part of the gain and returns to the risk she chose.

u13l6-6.prompt: Pablo is 22, has no emergency fund and owes €2,000 on his credit card. He wants to put €3,000 into crypto "because he's young and can take risks". What does he bear in mind?
options: That he should take out a loan to put in more
That the emergency fund and paying off expensive debt come first; then, if he decides to hold crypto, a portion he could afford to lose
That being young, the more risk he takes, the better
u13l6-6.explanation: Age gives you time, but it doesn't replace the basics: an emergency fund and no expensive debt.
feedback: Borrowing for crypto multiplies the risk of ending up worse off than when he started.
Good: the order matters. Credit card debt costs high interest for sure; crypto can be lost entirely.
With no cushion and expensive debt, a sharp fall could force him to sell at the worst moment or borrow even more.

u13l6-7.prompt: Put in order the steps before holding crypto in a portfolio.
options: A written plan with a maximum for crypto
Rebalancing if it goes over the maximum
u13l6-7.explanation: First the basics; then written rules; and finally, sticking to them when the market moves.
